```{python}
from research_site import Study

study = Study()
TRAIN = "Verse segmentation, training data"
TEST = "Verse segmentation, test data"
TRANSLATION = "Translation of held-out passages"
```

## Summary

- Oral Bible translation (OBT) projects get running text from speech recognition (ASR), which has to be **split into verses** before a machine translation (MT) model can train on it. Verse segmentation uses a word aligner, eflomal, whose results vary from run to run.
- Running eflomal several times and keeping the word links found in most runs **flagged fewer odd verses** in the training data: **251** (2.68%) with one run, **199** (2.12%) with 10 runs and **198** (2.11%) with 15. Most of the gain came by 10 runs.
- The gain is in verses whose target is much longer than the source (67 to 44) and in one-word verses (76 to 52). Verses much shorter than the source barely changed (141 to 134).
- **Translation quality did not change measurably.** chrF3 on held-out passages was 70.0 with one run and 70.3 to 70.6 with several. That is a gain of 0.2 to 0.6 points, within what one run on 17 passages can move.
- Removing the flagged training verses altogether did not help either: chrF3 was 69.7.

## The question

When ASR output is split into verses, a bad split gives a source verse that is paired with far too much or too little target text, and the MT model trains on that. The segmenter aligns the text with the published source Bible using eflomal, which trains a statistical model and so can give different alignments on different runs. Does running it several times and combining the results give better verse segmentation?

## The method

The segmenter runs eflomal N times and keeps a word link only if it appears in **more than half** of the runs. N is 1 for the baseline and 2, 5, 10 or 15 for the others.

For each setting, NLLB-200 was fine-tuned with silnlp on the verse-segmented ASR output for the New Testament, Genesis, Ruth and Jonah, paired verse by verse with a published Bible in a related language. All settings used the same ASR output, so only the verse boundaries differ.

A sixth experiment keeps the baseline segmentation and removes the verses flagged as odd (below) from the training data.

## How it was tested

**Translation.** Each model was scored at its 5,000-step checkpoint on **17 passages of Matthew 11 to 16**, using passage-level chrF3 and BLEU against the human transcriptions of the recordings.

**Segmentation quality.** There are no correct verse boundaries to compare with, so segmentation is judged by whether each target verse has a plausible length for its source verse. A verse is **flagged** if either:

- its length differs from the source verse's by at least 5 tokens and is an extreme outlier among all verses (a modified z-score of at least 10 on the length difference), whether the target is much longer or much shorter than the source, or
- its target has one token, or is empty (none were).

The **length correlation** is the Pearson correlation between source and target verse lengths. It is computed for the training data and for the Matthew 11 to 16 test data.

## Results

### Translation

```{python}
study.table(groups=[TRANSLATION], intervals=False, digits=2, group_title="Test")
```

All five variants score within 0.6 chrF3 of the baseline, and none is clearly better than another. BLEU differs by up to 0.8 and doesn't follow the number of runs. Each setting is one training run on 17 passages, so these differences are within the noise.

### Segmentation of the training data

```{python}
study.table(groups=[TRAIN], intervals=False, digits=2, group_title="Data")
```

- **More runs, fewer odd verses.** Flagged verses fell from 2.68% to 2.38% with 2 runs, 2.29% with 5, 2.12% with 10 and 2.11% with 15. The gains level off at 10 runs.
- **It is the long targets that improve.** Verses where the target is far longer than the source fell by about a third (0.72% to 0.47%), and one-word verses by about a third (0.81% to 0.55%). Verses where the target is far shorter than the source barely moved (1.51% to 1.43%).
- **The length correlation did not move** (0.09 for the baseline and for every run count). It is dominated by the few extreme verses: dropping the 251 flagged baseline verses lifts it from 0.09 to 0.86. Fixing about a fifth of them isn't enough to show.

### Segmentation of the test data

```{python}
study.table(groups=[TEST], intervals=False, digits=2, group_title="Data")
```

The test passages are short, so these counts are tiny: the baseline flags 2 of 235 verses and every multi-run setting 3 of 237. That is a difference of one verse, and tells us nothing about the effect of extra runs. The length correlation stays between 0.82 and 0.85.

### Removing flagged verses

The experiment with the 251 flagged training verses removed has no flagged verses left and a length correlation of 0.86. Its chrF3 is 69.7, 0.3 below the baseline, and its BLEU 30.0, 0.9 above. The two measures disagree, so removing the odd verses did not clearly help or hurt.

## Limitations

- **One run and 17 passages per setting.** There are no confidence intervals and no repeated training runs, so translation differences under about a point are not established.
- **A length check, not a boundary check.** A flagged verse is a suspicious one, and an unflagged verse can still have the wrong boundary. Better segmentation here means fewer implausible lengths, not more correct boundaries.
- **One language and one corpus.** The results describe a single project's speech recognition output and a single source Bible.
- **The test data is small.** Its segmentation statistics rest on two or three verses.

## Reproducing this

The results come from:

```{python}
study.provenance()
```
